questions.question: Which of these is found in both a bacterial cell and a plant cell? A a cell wall containing peptidoglycan, B linear chromosomes of DNA associated with histone proteins, C ribosomes, D mitochondria
steps: All cells make proteins, so both bacterial and plant cells have ribosomes (smaller 70S ribosomes in bacteria, larger 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm of plant cells).
A is wrong: bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan, but plant cell walls are made of cellulose.
B is wrong: bacteria have a single circular chromosome of DNA that is not associated with histones.
D is wrong: bacteria have no membrane-bound organelles, so they have no mitochondria.

questions.question: Penicillin stops growing bacteria from forming the cross-links in the peptidoglycan of their cell walls. Why does this kill the bacteria? A the cells can no longer carry out translation, B the weakened wall cannot withstand water entering by osmosis so the cells burst, C the cells can no longer replicate their DNA, D the plasmids in the cells are destroyed
questions.answer: B: the weakened wall cannot withstand water entering by osmosis so the cells burst.
steps: The wall of a bacterial cell stops the cell bursting as water enters by osmosis.
If new cross-links cannot form, the wall of a growing cell is weak, so it cannot resist the osmotic pressure and the cell bursts (lysis).
A and C describe the actions of other antibiotics (affecting ribosomes or DNA enzymes), not penicillin.
D is wrong: penicillin does not destroy plasmids. Human cells have no cell wall, so they are not affected.

questions.question: State two differences between a virus and a bacterium.
questions.answer: Any two: virus acellular, bacterium a cell; virus reproduces only in host cells, bacterium by binary fission; capsid versus cell wall; size; genetic material.
steps: A virus is acellular (no cytoplasm or ribosomes), whereas a bacterium is a cell with cytoplasm and ribosomes
A virus reproduces only inside a host cell, whereas a bacterium divides independently by binary fission
accept: A virus has a protein coat (capsid), whereas a bacterium has a cell wall (peptidoglycan)
A virus is much smaller than a bacterium
A virus has DNA or RNA, whereas a bacterium has DNA (circular chromosome and plasmids)
Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses

questions.question: Explain how the overuse of antibiotics can lead to an increase in the number of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in a population.
questions.answer: Chance mutation gives resistance; antibiotic selects for resistant bacteria, which reproduce and spread the allele (also on plasmids); overuse increases selection.
steps: Resistance arises by chance (random) mutation, giving a few bacteria an allele for resistance
The antibiotic is a selection pressure: non-resistant bacteria are killed but resistant ones survive
Resistant bacteria reproduce by binary fission with less competition and pass the allele to their offspring, so its frequency increases
Resistance genes on plasmids can be passed to other bacteria, including other species (by conjugation)
Overuse (e.g. for viral infections, incomplete courses) exposes more bacteria to the antibiotic, so selection is stronger and resistant bacteria spread
accept: Resistant bacteria spread between people or animals (e.g. in hospitals)
Routine use of antibiotics in farming exposes more bacteria to them
The allele may code for an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic (e.g. penicillinase)
The allele may alter the target site of the antibiotic

questions.question: A culture of Escherichia coli was grown in nutrient broth at 37 deg C. During the exponential phase the number of cells doubled at regular intervals. Explain why the number of bacteria increases exponentially during this phase.
questions.answer: Binary fission doubles the number each generation; nutrients are plentiful and waste low, so division is at its maximum rate.
steps: Each bacterium divides by binary fission into two cells, so the number doubles in each generation
Nutrients (and oxygen) are plentiful and little waste has built up, so division is at its maximum rate and few cells die
accept: The more cells there are, the more cells divide, so the increase gets larger each time
The temperature is close to the optimum for the enzymes, so division is rapid
No limiting factors/competition at this stage

questions.question: During the exponential phase, the number of Escherichia coli cells in a culture increased from 3.2 x 10^4 cells cm^-3 to 2.0 x 10^8 cells cm^-3 in 5.0 hours. The growth rate constant, k, is the number of generations per hour: k = (log10 Nt - log10 N0) / (0.301 x t), where N0 is the number of cells at the start, Nt is the number of cells after time t, and t is in hours. Calculate k for this culture, to two significant figures.
steps: k = 2.5 generations per hour (2 s.f.) (1).

questions.question: After the exponential phase, the number of living Escherichia coli cells in a culture in nutrient broth stopped increasing and stayed constant for several hours. Explain why the number of living cells stopped increasing.
questions.answer: Nutrients run low and toxic waste builds up, so the division rate falls until it equals the death rate.
steps: Nutrients (and oxygen) are being used up, which limits growth
Toxic waste products (e.g. acids) accumulate and lower the pH, which limits growth
The rate of cell division falls until it equals the rate of cell death, so the number of living cells stays constant
accept: Increased competition for space and resources between the cells
Enzyme activity falls as the pH becomes unsuitable
This is the stationary phase of the growth curve

questions.question: A student spread a bacterium over sterile nutrient agar in a Petri dish and placed paper discs soaked in antibiotic on the agar. The lid of the dish was held on with two small pieces of tape and the dish was incubated at 25 deg C rather than 37 deg C. Explain why the dish was not sealed completely and was incubated at 25 deg C.
questions.answer: Not sealed so oxygen enters and anaerobic pathogens cannot grow; 25 deg C is below body temperature so human pathogens grow poorly.
steps: Lid not fully sealed so oxygen can enter, which prevents the growth of anaerobic bacteria (which may be pathogens)
25 deg C is lower than body temperature (37 deg C), so pathogens adapted to the human body are less likely to grow
accept: Tape holds the lid on to stop contamination from the air while allowing gas exchange
Sealed, anaerobic conditions favour dangerous anaerobic pathogens
Incubating at 37 deg C would encourage growth of human pathogens

questions.question: Paper discs soaked in antibiotic P or antibiotic Q were placed on agar spread with bacteria and incubated. After 48 hours there was a circular clear zone with no bacterial growth around each disc. The clear zone around the disc with antibiotic P had a diameter of 16 mm and the clear zone around the disc with antibiotic Q had a diameter of 10 mm. Calculate how many times greater the area of the clear zone around P is than the area of the clear zone around Q.
steps: Radius of clear zone P = 8 mm, so area = pi x 8^2 = 201 mm^2 (1).
Radius of clear zone Q = 5 mm, so area = pi x 5^2 = 78.5 mm^2 (1).
Area P / area Q = 201 / 78.5 = 2.56, so the area around P is 2.56 times greater (1).

questions.question: The clear zone around a disc of antibiotic P had an area 2.56 times greater than the clear zone around a disc of antibiotic Q. A student concluded that P is 2.56 times as effective as Q at killing the bacteria. Explain why this conclusion may not be valid.
questions.answer: Any two: zone size depends on diffusion rate; amounts on the discs may differ; clear zone does not show killing; only one trial.
steps: The size of the clear zone depends on how far each antibiotic diffuses through the agar (e.g. molecular size), not only on its effectiveness
The amounts or concentrations of the antibiotics on the discs may differ, so it is not a fair comparison
accept: A clear zone shows growth was prevented, not whether bacteria were killed (bactericidal) or only stopped from growing (bacteriostatic)
Only one trial was done, so reliability is not known and no statistical test was possible
The area of the zone is not directly proportional to the effectiveness of the antibiotic
The bacterial lawn may have been uneven

questions.question: Rigor mortis develops after death because A lactic acid builds up and causes the myosin to contract, B ATP is no longer produced so the myosin heads cannot detach from the actin, C nerve impulses continue to stimulate the muscles, D the fall in body temperature denatures the actin
questions.answer: B: ATP is no longer produced so the myosin heads cannot detach from the actin.
steps: After death respiration stops, so no more ATP is made.
ATP is needed to break the cross-bridges between myosin heads and actin, so the muscles stay contracted and become stiff.
A is wrong: lactic acid does not cause myosin to contract. C is wrong: nerve impulses stop after death.
D is wrong: a fall in temperature does not denature actin in this way. Rigor passes later as the muscle proteins break down.

questions.question: One double-stranded DNA molecule is amplified using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). How many double-stranded DNA molecules are there after 6 complete cycles? A 12, B 36, C 64, D 128
steps: The number of molecules doubles in every cycle, so after n cycles the number is 2^n.
A is wrong: 12 is 6 x 2, which treats the increase as linear.
B is wrong: 36 is 6^2, and D is wrong: 128 is 2^7, which is one cycle too many.

questions.question: Describe how the insects found on a corpse can be used to estimate the time of death.
questions.answer: Find the oldest insect stage and its length, use the temperature at the scene and known development times to work back to when eggs were laid.
steps: Blowflies are attracted soon after death and lay eggs on the body, so the age of the oldest insects gives a minimum time since death
Identify the species and stage of the life cycle (egg, larva, pupa) and measure the length of the largest larvae
Record the temperature at the scene, as development rate depends on temperature, and compare with known development times for that species
Calculate the time taken for the oldest stage to develop, giving the time the eggs were laid, which is close to the time of death
accept: Succession: different species arrive at different stages of decomposition, so the species present indicate the time since death
Beetles and other species arrive later than blowflies
Empty pupal cases show that the life cycle has been completed, so a longer time since death

questions.question: A body was found in a house at 06:00. The core body temperature was 25.0 deg C. Normal core body temperature is 37.0 deg C. Assume that, after death, the body cooled at a constant rate of 1.5 deg C per hour. Calculate the estimated time of death.
steps: Fall in temperature = 37.0 - 25.0 = 12.0 deg C.
Time since death = 12.0 / 1.5 = 8.0 hours.
Time of death = 06:00 - 8 hours = 22:00 on the previous day.

questions.question: The time of death of a person was estimated from the core body temperature, assuming that the body cooled at a constant 1.5 deg C per hour from 37.0 deg C. Suggest three reasons why this estimate of the time of death may be inaccurate.
questions.answer: Any three: surroundings/clothing; body size and fat; starting temperature not 37.0 deg C; cooling rate not constant.
steps: The cooling rate depends on the temperature of the surroundings, air movement and whether the body was clothed or covered
The cooling rate depends on the size of the body and the amount of fat (surface area to volume ratio, insulation)
The temperature at death may not have been 37.0 deg C (e.g. fever or exercise)
accept: Cooling is not constant: there is an initial delay and the rate slows as the body nears the temperature of the surroundings
The body position (curled up or spread out) changes the surface area exposed
The body may have been moved after death
Error in the temperature measurement (where in the body it was taken)

questions.question: Forensic scientists estimating the time of death may use body temperature, the stage of rigor mortis and the insects present on the body. Explain why they use evidence from more than one of these sources.
questions.answer: Each method is affected by other variables and works only for a limited time; independent methods that agree give more confidence and a narrower range.
steps: Each method is affected by other variables (e.g. temperature of the surroundings alters cooling, rigor mortis and insect development)
Each method is reliable only for a limited period (body temperature about a day, rigor mortis a day or two, insects days to weeks)
Results from independent methods can be compared; agreement gives more confidence in the estimate
Combining them gives a narrower range of times, and a result that disagrees can be investigated
accept: Different methods suit different times since death, so together they cover a longer period
One method may not be available (e.g. no insects present indoors or in winter)
Anomalies or errors in one estimate can be identified

questions.question: Explain why the decomposition of a heap of garden waste is faster when the heap is warm, moist and well aerated than when it is cold and waterlogged.
questions.answer: Warmth speeds enzyme action and decomposer growth; water is needed for growth and hydrolysis; oxygen allows aerobic respiration; waterlogging excludes oxygen.
steps: Warmth gives enzyme and substrate molecules more kinetic energy, so more collisions and enzyme-substrate complexes, so the decomposers digest the waste faster
Decomposers (saprotrophic bacteria and fungi) grow and reproduce faster when warm, so more enzymes are secreted
Water is needed for the growth of decomposers and for hydrolysis (digestion) reactions
A well-aerated heap has oxygen for aerobic respiration, which releases more energy for growth; a waterlogged heap has little oxygen, so decomposition is slower
accept: In cold conditions enzymes have too little kinetic energy, so activity is low
Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose, so less growth
Too much water reduces the diffusion of oxygen into the heap

questions.question: A small bloodstain was found at a crime scene. The DNA in the stain was amplified using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Describe how PCR is used to produce many copies of the DNA from the stain.
questions.answer: Mix DNA with primers, nucleotides and Taq polymerase; 95 deg C to separate strands, 55 deg C for primers to anneal, 72 deg C for extension; repeat the cycle.
steps: The DNA is mixed with primers, free nucleotides and a heat-stable DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase) in a buffer
Heat to about 95 deg C to break the hydrogen bonds and separate the two strands
Cool to about 55 deg C so that the primers anneal to the complementary sequences on each single strand
Heat to about 72 deg C, the optimum for Taq polymerase, which adds nucleotides to the primers to make new strands; repeat the cycle many times, doubling the DNA each cycle
accept: The cycles are carried out in a thermocycler
Taq polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus) is not denatured at 95 deg C
Primers are short single-stranded DNA sequences complementary to the ends of the target region
An annealing temperature of 50 to 65 deg C is accepted

questions.question: A DNA profile was produced from a bloodstain at a crime scene using short tandem repeats (STRs), which are short sequences of non-coding DNA repeated a variable number of times. It was compared with the DNA profiles of two suspects. Explain how the profiles could show that the blood came from one of the suspects.
questions.answer: STRs vary in repeat number between people; fragments separated by size by gel electrophoresis; a suspect matching the stain at every STR is the likely source.
steps: The number of repeats at each STR differs between people, so the DNA fragments amplified by PCR from different people differ in length
The fragments are separated by size by gel electrophoresis, giving a pattern of bands for each person
The suspect whose bands match the stain at all the STRs tested is the likely source, as the probability of an unrelated person matching at every STR is very small
accept: The fragments are made visible with a fluorescent or radioactive label or a DNA stain
A suspect with a band that is missing from the stain is excluded
The more STRs tested, the smaller the probability of a chance match
